December 2009 Vol 37 No 6 ## Copper mine production from the late 1990s – A paradox? _page 2_ Mine and mill capacity is a contentious issue and the cause of much debate. The amount of copper metal a mine produces depends on ore tonnages mined (itself determined by the number of hours worked each year), ore grade and recovery rates of the processes used to extract the copper contained in the ore. In this article, Phillip Crowson, Honorary Professor and a part-time Professorial Research Fellow at CEPMLP, The University of Dundee, looks at mine production over the period between 1999 and 2007. Statistics show that global mine output fell increasingly short of estimated capacity over the past decade. There are a number of possible reasons for this. Firstly, are there deficiencies in the data? Mine capacity is not an easy number to determine. Secondly, underperformance by two of the world’s largest mines – Grasberg and Escondida – since 2002, has contributed to the shortfall. Thirdly, on a geographical basis most copper producing countries experienced declines in rates of capacity utilisation, mainly due to an increase in labour militancy in response to the high copper price since 2004. Fourthly, in recent years copper mines may have maximised their output of co- and by-products at the expense of copper. Finally, ore grades have been cited at a number of mines as a reason for lower production levels. Ore grades will decline over time at a mine unless new and higher grade reserves are found and delineated. Taken together, these factors may have reduced utilisation by as much as 10% in recent years. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 2 # Copper mine production from the late 1990s – A paradox? ### The basic issue Between 1998 and 2008 the estimated capacity of the world’s copper mines increased by almost 5.8 million tonnes, or 45%. This compares with the 4.5 million tonne, or 33%, growth in the total usage of refined copper over the same period and the 3.9 million tonne (34%) increase in the usage of primary refined copper (i.e. total usage less production of secondary refined copper). This implies that the mining companies responded effectively to rising demand and prices by investing in ample new and replacement mine capacity. Even before allowing for any rise in the usage of secondary refined metal, there should, therefore, have been more than enough supplies of mined copper to meet rising demand and ensure market balance. Trends in mine capacity and usage of refined copper since 1998 are shown in figure 1. ##### **Figure 1** Copper usage, mine capacity and output, 1998 to 2008

In practice, as figure 1 also shows, global mine output fell increasingly short of estimated capacity during the decade. Mine output grew by only 3.2 million tonnes, or 26%, between 1998 and 2008. The implied percentage utilisation of global capacity is compared with the behaviour of copper prices (expressed in real 2007 terms) in figure 2. The percentage utilisation of global mine capacity had averaged 93.8% over the 1997-2001 period according to the International Copper Study Group (ICSG). It fell to about 90% in 2002-03 in a natural lagged response to weakening prices and picked up to 91% in 2004 with the revival of prices. So far, so good, but its subsequent performance appears aberrant. It dropped steadily in the 2005-07 period, notwithstanding the strong rises in real prices. It is this seemingly perverse drop in capacity utilisation when market conditions were strong that requires an explanation. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 3 ##### **Figure 2** Copper prices and mine capacity utilisation, 1998 to 2008

Recent rates appear to have been much lower than at any time in the preceding thirty years. ### Deficiencies in the data? One obvious possible explanation is that estimates of recent mine capacity might be incorrect. They are built up from a comprehensive database of individual mines, as are those of the International Wrought Copper Council (IWCC). The two series are compared in figure 4. ##### **Figure 4** Estimates of global copper mine capacity, 1999 to 2008

The IWCC estimates that global mine capacity grew more rapidly than suggested by the ICSG. In practice, this may not mean a great deal as the two organisations probably exchange data, but it does show that the ICSG is not out on a limb. It would have had to over-estimate total annual capacity by about 0.5 million tonnes in 2003-05, 0.8 million tonnes in 2006, and some 1.5 million tonnes in 2007 for the utilisation rate merely to have maintained its average level of the preceding thirty years. It is notoriously difficult to estimate the annual capacity of mines to produce contained metal. Mines extract ore and waste rather than metal, and their capacity is strictly the tonnage of material that they can move and process each year. In all mines that depends on the number of days and hours worked. At one extreme, some plan on continuous 365-day operation, whereas others may normally work just two shifts and operate for only part of each week. Where the climate is adverse some may close down for part of the year, and the length of closures will vary each year with the weather. Estimates of the capacity of each individual mine will normally reflect its standard working practices. In open-pit operations the tonnage moved depends on the number and size of shovels and trucks, and the scale and nature of the milling and processing facilities. Underground mines are further constrained by their need to raise material from their working faces to the surface for treatment. As a mine goes deeper, the volume of waste rock extracted will tend to increase. Unless continuing inve

stment is made in the necessary equipment, the scope to produce and process ore will tend to diminish over time.  Where the estimated capacity of mines to produce metal remains constant over long periods, there is an implicit assumption that the additional equipment required is readily available. 

© 2009 CRU International Limited confidential 

<u>www.crumonitor.com</u> COPPER STUDIES December 2009 

5 

Even assuming that mine managements always carefully plan operations to optimise their utilisation of equipment, the output of metal will vary with the nature of the materials extracted.  Estimates of the capacity of mines to produce metal tend to assume constant ore grades, milling efficiencies and recovery rates.  Yet the nature and grades of ore will vary over time in many mines.  Furthermore there may be unforeseen discontinuities in the ore deposits worked.  Thus annual output of contained metal may fluctuate, even when the throughput of ore (and waste) remains constant. 

In many porphyry copper deposits initial production may be from an enriched zone with higher grades than the deposit’s average.  Moreover, companies will be keen to maximise their output in the early years of operation in order to enhance net present values.  Annual output of contained metals in the early years of a mine’s operation may, therefore, exceed the likely long-run average.  If mine capacity were rising at a steady rate, this tendency for the annual capacity to produce metal to settle below the output of the early years might not significantly bias estimates of overall mine capacity.  It becomes an issue, however, where investment in new mines is bunched, as it was in the late 1990s, and in more recent times.  Many large mines might have been producing above the capacity that could be sustained in the longer term without continuing investment in additional equipment.  Where global estimates of capacity do not recognise this, they will be biased upwards. 

Most estimates of capacity do allow for the staged build-up of output to nominal capacity, but another possible bias is too ready an acceptance of the predictions made in corporate press announcements.  Even under the most favourable conditions it takes time for new mines to build up to full capacity working, because of the need to tune plant and equipment and overcome teething problems of all types.  A study by Charles Rivers Associates for the World Bank in 1979 concluded that "new mines may be expected to have average annual production equal to 50% to 70% of the designed capacity during their first year from start up, 80% to 100% of designed capacity during their second year after start up, and at or near their designed capacity after the third year"<sup>1</sup> .  Mines are today entering production with much larger initial capacities than thirty years ago, and the running-in periods have probably extended.  Furthermore, those periods are likely to vary over the course of the business cycle, becoming more p

rotracted when times are buoyant and suppliers of all goods and services are under pressure. The times needed to attain full capacity are likely to be much greater for new mines than for expansions to existing mines, where many of the potential problems can be more clearly foreseen and overcome. As figure 5 shows, completely new mines have accounted for a greater share of additional capacity in the Western World since the early 1990s than in the two preceding decades. In summary, inadequate allowance for the time taken for new mines to reach full capacity, and failure to recognise the tendency for effective capacity to decline after a mine’s first few years, might have led to some over-estimation of global mine capacity in recent years. The methodology of estimating capacity does not appear to have changed over the much longer period, however, and neither factor appears to have significantly affected estimates of capacity in previous cycles. Yet the number of mines has fallen considerably and the average scale of new mines has risen, both absolutely and relative to existing capacity. Over-estimates for a limited number of new mines could have a much more pronounced effect on estimates of the total than in earlier cycles. Figure 6, which compares the development of capacity and output for selected large new mines that opened from 1994 onwards, sheds some light. There are two sets of data, the first for seven mines – Alumbrera in Argentina, Sossego in Brazil, and Collahuasi, El Abra, La Candelaria

, Los Pelambres open pit and Zaldivar, all in Chile. Their combined output has never fallen below 91% of their capacity, and in most years their utilisation rate was substantially higher. Peru’s Antamina and Indonesia’s Batu Hijau are the additions in the set of nine mines. Their output has fallen increasingly short of estimated capacity since 2004, but the shortfall may reflect operational difficulties of various types rather than faulty estimates of capacity. The nine mines together accounted for nearly 12% of global (less Chinese) capacity in 2007. Figure 6 suggests that over-estimates of the capacity of new mines contributed to recent trends in utilisation rates, but are not a full explanation. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 7 ##### **Figure 6** Selected new copper mines' capacity and output,

That would have raised global capacity utilisation close to its longer-term average in 2003-04, but would have still meant below average utilisation in 2006-07. The shortfalls in these two mines come from a mixture of over-estimation of their capacity, through undue reliance on corporate statements of intent, and various operating difficulties they experienced after 2002. In the latter regard they were not alone, as shown by the widespread nature of the fall in utilisation rates. ### Geographical distribution of capacity and output The geographical distribution of es

There was a well-documented rise in labour militancy in response to buoyant copper prices and mine profitability from 2004 onwards. Coming after many years of quiescence, this resulted in an increased incidence of strikes and labour disruptions. Prominent examples included strikes at Mexico’s La Caridad and Cananea mines in 2006-07 which reduced their combined annual output by some 65,000-75,000 tonnes. The effects of labour unrest were additional to the usual disruptions caused by natural events such as abnormal weather and earthquakes. There was no obvious rise in such natural disruptions, but their impact is less easily absorbed when mines are trying to maximise their output than when product markets are less buoyant. © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 10 The 2004-07 economic upswing was much stronger and more widespread than any since the early 1970s, affecting nearly all industries simultaneously. Suppliers of maintenance spares, tyres and equipment were unable to satisfy an unexpectedly strong surge in demand. Not only did the costs of equipmen

t rise sharply, but delivery times were greatly extended. For example, ABARE noted in June 2008 that delivery times for haul truck tyres, and for large haul trucks themselves, had lengthened from a normal three months to two years2 . Such extended delivery times would have had an impact on some mines’ ability to sustain their output at planned rates, and would have contributed to the fall in utilisation rates. If extended lead times for spares and equipment were important contributors to shortfalls in mine output from expected rates, then their effects should die away during 2009 as a consequence of recession. Were there, however, any other general influences involved? ### By-product emphases? One possibility that received some attention in 2005-06 was that copper mines maximised their output of by- and co-products at copper’s expense. Their ore throughput may have been maintained, but its copper content may have fallen because mines were concentrating on other, more profitable metals. In that regard, molybdenum was the metal most frequently quoted. It occurs in many of the porphyry copper deposits of the Southwestern USA and in Chile and Peru. Figure 9 compares the ratio of molybdenum to copper production in the mines that produced both copper and molybdenum with the ratio of the prices of molybdenum (molybdic oxide in concentrate) and copper metal. ##### **Figure 9** The sharp jump in relative molybdenum prices in 2004-05 was associated with a rise in the relative output of molybdenum. Mines with existing molybdenum circuits boosted their production, and some mines with potential molybdenum began molybdenum recovery. Whilst many mines were not able to juggle their production schedules to raise molybdenum output differentially, some could. Had their output of copper merely risen at the same pace as their ore production, copper-molybdenum mines would have produced about 0.3 million tonnes per annum of additional copper in 2003-06, and almost 0.5 million tonnes extra in 2007. The global rates of capacity utilisation would have been 1.5-2 percentage points higher in 2003-06 and some 3 percentage points higher in 2007. As neither Escondida nor Grasberg produced molybdenum, this effect is additional to their shortfalls noted earlier. The evidence, therefore, supports the assertion that copper production suffered from the strength of molybdenum markets, but that does not explain the fall in utilisation rates in countries without copper-molybdenum mines. ### Ore grades Escondida’s management cited falling ore grades as one reason for sluggish output in recent years. Might changes in ore grades provide a more general explanation for output falling increasingly short of nominal capacity? Figure 13 compares annual head grades, ignoring any by-product values, from 1996 onwards – first for major Chilean mines and then for selected large mines in other countries – with annual average LME prices for copper, expressed in real 2007 terms (using the US implicit GDP price deflator). The mines shown collectively accounted for 41% of non-Chinese copper mine output in 2005. The fall in Escondida’s grade up to 2005 (before some recovery in 2007) is the most pronounced, with Collahuasi and Olympic Dam also showing large falls. Collahuasi managed to sustain its output despite falling grades, but Olympic Dam’s production fell short of its nominal capacity in 2003, and again in 2005-07. Grasberg’s copper grade moved erratically, one reason for its production shortfalls. On the one hand it might be argued that mines will exploit higher grade segments of their ore deposits when prices are high and lower grade segments when prices are low, in order to enhance net present values by producing and selling more when prices are high. An alternative, and widely held, view is that miners extract lower grade ores when prices are high in order to maximise the amount of useful product extracted over the life of a mine whilst maintaining profitability. The data used in this paper cover too short a period, and too narrow a range of mines, to determine whether there has been any general and consistent relationship between the grades of ore treated and prices. Specific examples aside, changes in ore grades do not appear to explain why mine output has fallen short of nominal capacity. In many instances declines in ore grades were long predicted, and were offset by increases in milling capacity in order to sustain the output of contained copper. It does not appear that higher prices from 2004 onwards encouraged the mines of figure 13 to raise their head grades in order to maximise their returns. Equally, weak prices in earlier years do not appear to have led either to widespread high-grading, or to policy-driven falls in head grades. Notwithstanding the ‘molybdenum effect’ noted earlier, the mining plans of most large open-pit copper mines tend to lack the flexibility to © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 14 vary their grades in the short-run in response to price changes. This table is merely illustrative, as the precise impact of each factor is not precisely known. The first three lines of table 3 contain the data on global mine capacity and output published by the ICSG. The subsequent five lines show the implied reductions in potential output caused by the specified factors. The first is the additional copper that would have been produced had copper output at copper- © 2009 CRU International Limited confidential www.crumonitor.com COPPER STUDIES December 2009 15 molybdenum mines risen at the same pace as their mill throughput from 2002 onwards. The next shows the annual shortfall in the combined output of Escondida and Grasberg from a steady 95% of nominal capacity. That rate is rather below the average of the preceding decade. For Batu Hijau and Olympic Dam the shortfalls are more conservatively taken from 90% utilisation. Even taking all these factors into account, the rate of global mine utilisation would have fallen short of its historic average in 2005-07, a period of buoyant prices.  The extra output needed to take utilisation up to 95% of stated capacity is shown in the penultimate line of the table.  This would cover influences such as over-estimates of capacity for smaller mines, losses in output caused by disruptions of all types, and the impact of extended lead times for spares and equipment. 

Much of the gap between the implied potential and actual output is unlikely ever to be bridged until more precise (and lower) estimates of effective capacity are made.  Some 0.5-1.0 million tonnes in 2007 does, however, appear to have been temporary, and likely to be eliminated in due course.  Lead times for delivery of supplies and equipment have contracted, and labour unrest has eased with the fall in copper prices.  Meantime, weakened profitability and reduced demand have led to production cutbacks and some mine closures, so that utilisation rates have remained low.  That is, however, for voluntary market-based reasons, rather than forced by circumstances.

Our agenda is flexible and we would also welcome suggestions and ideas from our readers.  During 2010 we hope to include some if not all of the articles listed below:
